title: A pretty dashboard isn't enough: how to design data that helps people decide
description: A well-designed dashboard can still help no one decide. Start with the question, give the number context and organize around the decision.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: product interfaces that turn operational data into signals the team can interpret.

blocks.text: A dashboard can have good hierarchy, consistent charts and a well-chosen palette and still not help anyone make a decision.
That happens when the dashboard shows what's easy to measure, but doesn't make clear what changed, why it matters or which question needs to be investigated.
The goal of a product dashboard isn't to display as much data as possible. It's to shorten the time between noticing a signal and deciding what to do next.
Start with the business question

Before choosing charts, define who will use the dashboard and what decision they need to make. Product leadership may need to understand whether activation is improving. Growth may be investigating which funnel step saw conversion drop. Design may compare task completion before and after a change.

These questions call for different views. A dashboard that tries to answer everything ends up with no clear priority. For each visualization, write a question in plain language. If you can't explain what decision the chart supports, maybe it doesn't need to be on the main dashboard.
Give the number context

“Conversion: 4.2%” leaves questions open. Did that number go up or down? Compared to which period? What's the sample size? Did the traffic mix change? Is there a defined target? Is the difference meaningful for the business or could it be normal variation?

A good dashboard helps answer these without forcing someone to open several tools. Include the period, a relevant comparison, the metric definition and, when needed, the observed volume. Avoid green or red arrows without explaining the rule used to define better or worse.
Choose the chart based on the question

items: Funnel: show the steps of a journey and where drop-off happens.
Scatter: explore the relationship between two variables, without assuming causation.
Table: look up precise values or compare several attributes.
Cohort: compare groups that started in different periods and track retention or behavior.

blocks.text: Don't pick a chart because it's trendy or looks sophisticated. Pick the format that makes the comparison easier and doesn't distort the reading.
Show the signal, but don't pretend to know the cause

If conversion dropped after an interface change, there's a temporal association. That doesn't prove the change caused the drop. The dashboard can highlight when the behavior changed and allow segmenting by device, channel or user type. The cause needs to be investigated with additional context, instrumentation checks, research or appropriate experiments.
Organize the hierarchy by importance
One possible structure:

items: Main outcome: the metric that represents the goal.
Explanatory indicators: funnel steps or related behaviors.
Relevant segments: device, channel, user type or plan.
Guardrail metrics: signals of quality, errors or side effects.
Detail: a table or complementary exploration.

blocks.text: The hierarchy should follow the team's decisions, not a fixed visual formula. Avoid filling the first screen with cards that compete with each other.
Accessibility improves analysis too

Poor contrast, small labels, truncated axes and relying only on red and green make interpretation harder. Use direct labels, consistent scales, visible units and annotations that explain important changes. Don't rely on color alone to tell series apart: combine color with labels, shapes, patterns or line styles. Test readability on desktop and mobile.
A dashboard needs to lead to a next action
A good visualization can end with a question to investigate, not an automatic conclusion.

cards.v: the drop shows up mostly on mobile devices.
did the interaction change, or the profile of people arriving on mobile?
check events, reproduce the flow and observe real users.

data.close: The dashboard doesn't replace analysis. It helps direct it.
